title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 183
paragraphs: From Augila, at another distance of ten days' journey, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, with a great number of fruit-bearing date-palms, as in the other places; and people live here who are called the Garamantes, a very great nation, who carry earth to spread over the salt and then sow crops. From this point the shortest route is to the Lotus-eaters, for from them it is a thirty days' journey to the country of the Garamantes. Among them too are produced the cattle that graze backwards; and they graze backwards for this reason: they have horns that bend down forward, and so they walk backwards as they feed—for they cannot go forward, because their horns would drive into the ground in front of them. In no other respect do they differ from ordinary cattle, except in this and in the thickness and firmness of their hide. These Garamantes of whom I speak hunt the “Cave-dwelling” Ethiopians in their four-horse chariots, for the Cave-dwelling Ethiopians are the swiftest-footed of all people we hear tell of; and the Cave-dwellers feed on snakes and lizards and such creeping things, and they use a language unlike any other—in it they squeak just like bats.
